note: Promotion to the tracked schema (roadmap Phase 1 backfill). Track groups follow the (XX) prefixes already embedded in the source theme names; only empty fields (track, code, level, description) are filled — source themes, credentials and transfer checks are untouched.

themes.description: Reading a real utility or service bill line by line — what is owed, by when, and what happens if it is ignored.
Where water and electricity enter the home, how the meter counts them, and shutting either off safely.

themes.theme: A room that can be cleaned (HH)
themes.description: The order and method of cleaning a room so it stays clean — surfaces, floors, and the corners that get skipped.
The household repairs anyone can do — a washer, a fuse, a hinge — and recognising the ones that need a professional.
Sorting, temperatures, dosing and drying so clothes come out clean and last — including washing by hand.
Reading the early signs of pests and damp, the causes behind them, and the response that stops them spreading.

themes.theme: The household that runs on a list (HH)
themes.description: Shopping lists, chore rotas and the weekly routine — running a household deliberately instead of by crisis.
The agreements that make shared kitchens, bathrooms and bills workable, and repairing them when they break.
The household emergencies — leak, outage, lockout, gas smell — and the first correct move for each.
Moving out well: notice, cleaning, meter readings, key handover and getting the deposit back.
Tracking a real month of spending until the pattern is visible, and naming the categories honestly.

themes.theme: The account, the card and the fee (MY)
themes.description: What a basic account does, what a card actually is, and the fees that quietly take from small balances.
Interest as the price of borrowed money — comparing a loan, a card and an informal lender on total cost.
Checking pay against hours and rate, reading the deductions, and querying a shortfall without drama.

themes.theme: Saving where you cannot reach it (MY)
themes.description: Why savings survive only when they are separated, and the vehicles — account, lockbox, club — that create distance.
The frauds that target ordinary money — prizes, urgent transfers, fake officials — and the checks that defeat them.
Cost per use, quality signals and timing — spending more once instead of less repeatedly.

themes.theme: Tax, in the simplest form that is true (MY)
themes.description: What tax is, which ones touch your life, and the difference between avoiding a form and owing a debt.
Lending to and borrowing from family and friends with terms said out loud, and what a gift is.

themes.theme: Planning for the month that goes wrong (MY)
themes.description: The buffer, the priority order of bills, and who to call first when income stops.
The identity and qualification papers work requires, where each comes from, and keeping copies that survive.

themes.theme: Filling in a form that decides something (WK)
themes.description: Reading a consequential form fully before writing, answering what is actually asked, and keeping the copy.

themes.theme: Writing to somebody who can help (WK)
themes.description: The short, specific letter or message — who you are, what you need, by when — that gets an answer.
Researching the role, preparing three stories and two questions, and arriving early in the right clothes.
Names, rules, where things are and what to ask — the first day handled so the second is easier.

themes.theme: Being paid to do a job well (WK)
themes.description: Reliability, standards and finishing — the working habits that turn a job into a reference.

themes.theme: When something goes wrong at work (WK)
themes.description: Mistakes, conflicts and accidents at work — owning, reporting and repairing them in the right order.
The minimum wage, hours, breaks and safety rules that apply where you live, and where to turn when they are broken.
Pricing, invoicing, records and tax when you are the business — the paperwork that keeps small work legitimate.
Notice, handover and the reference — ending a job so the door stays open.

tracks.name: Getting things done in the world

themes.theme: Reading a timetable and a map (CM)
themes.description: Planning a real journey from timetable and map alone — connections, walking legs and the margin for error.
The checks and small maintenance that keep a bicycle, motorbike or car dependable, and the costs of neglect.
Working backwards from an appointment — preparation, travel and buffer — so arriving early becomes ordinary.
Booking with a clinic, office or service: the information to have ready, the questions to ask, and the confirmation to keep.
Stating your business to an official clearly and calmly — what to bring, what to ask for, and what to write down after.
Dates, names, reference numbers and copies — the personal record-keeping that wins disputes months later.
Naming what you need, choosing who to ask, and accepting help in a way that keeps your dignity and theirs.

themes.theme: Doing something for the first time (CM)
themes.description: The method for any unfamiliar task — find someone who has done it, break it down, do the first small step today.

themes.theme: When you are the responsible adult (CM)
themes.description: Being the one in charge of children, elders or a situation — the duties that arrive with the role and the calls you must be ready to make.

themes.theme: Teaching somebody else what you learned (CM)
themes.description: Passing on a skill properly — showing, watching them try, and correcting without taking over.

tracks.name: The first minutes of an emergency

themes.description: The look-assess-act habit at any emergency — danger first, then the person, then the call.
The emergency numbers where you live, what the call-taker will ask, and giving a location that can be found.
Direct pressure, elevation and when a bleed is beyond home control — stopping blood loss with what is in reach.
Recognising true choking and delivering back blows and thrusts, adapted for infants and adults.
Cooling a burn long enough, covering it right, and the burns that must be seen by a clinician.
Checking response and breathing, the recovery position, and staying until help takes over.
Escape first, doors closed, smoke low — the household fire response, and the small fire you may fight.
The drowning risks around your own area, reach-and-throw rescue, and why swimmers drown trying to help.
Crossing, riding and travelling defensively, and the first-on-scene basics at a road accident.
The hours after — reporting, records, checking on people, and the reactions in yourself that are normal.
